# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has transformed the management of severe aortic stenosis, but its delivery depends on large-bore vascular access. Transcatheter aortic valve replacement necessitates a large-bore access, most commonly accomplished through transfemoral arterial access; however, a subset of patients, up to 5%, may exhibit insufficient iliofemoral diameters and require alternative approaches. [1] Historically, alternatives have included transapical and transaortic (transthoracic) access, but transthoracic access is inferior compared with femoral-artery access, perhaps in part because of the clinical features precluding femoral artery access. [2,3] Transcaval access emerged as a fully percutaneous, nonthoracic alternative for these patients.

## Concept and Rationale

Transcaval aortic access is a versatile electrosurgical technique for large-bore arterial access through the wall of the abdominal aorta from the adjoining inferior vena cava. Although counterintuitive, its relative safety derives from the recognition that interstitial hydraulic pressure exceeds venous pressure, so arterial bleeding harmlessly decompresses into the nearby caval venous hole. [4] The approach was first validated preclinically, demonstrating that large therapeutic devices can be introduced into the aorta via the IVC in a simple catheter procedure, and the fistula closed uneventfully despite full anticoagulation. [5] Technically, from the femoral vein, an electrified guidewire is directed from the inferior vena cava into a snare prepositioned into the adjoining abdominal aorta; after guidewire exchange, the standard introducer sheath is then advanced from the femoral vein into the abdominal aorta, allowing retrograde TAVR to be performed as usual. [6] A central advantage is that, unlike other alternative access TAVR techniques, transcaval access facilitates the same ergonomics as traditional transfemoral arterial access TAVR. [1]

## Early Clinical Experience

The first-in-human series established feasibility, delivering large sheaths into the abdominal aorta via the femoral vein and IVC, with the tract closed using nitinol occluders. [7] A prospective, multicenter Investigational Device Exemption trial followed: a prospective, independently-adjudicated, multi-center, single-arm trial of transcaval access for TAVR in patients ineligible for femoral artery access and at high or prohibitive risk from transthoracic access enrolled 100 subjects who underwent attempted percutaneous transcaval access by electrifying a caval guidewire and advancing into a prepositioned aortic snare. [8] In that cohort, transcaval access enabled TAVR in patients who were not good candidates for transthoracic access, although bleeding and vascular complications, using permeable nitinol cardiac occluders to close the access ports, were common but acceptable in this high-risk cohort. [8]

## Procedural Planning and Closure

Careful imaging is essential. Transcaval access is a new approach to introduce large devices, such as transcatheter aortic valves, into the abdominal aorta in patients who otherwise lack access options. [9] Dedicated step-by-step guidance has been published for planning and executing the procedure and remedying complications. [10] Computed tomography is the cornerstone of target selection, teaching operators how to plan transcaval access and closure based on cross-sectional anatomy, including calcium-free target selection. [11] Best-practice consensus emphasizes that with meticulous CT planning and by following the technical steps described, transcaval access offers a safe, nonfemoral access route for TAVR and for other interventions that require large-bore arterial access. [4] The technique exemplifies transcatheter electrosurgery, which refers to a family of procedures using radiofrequency energy to vaporize and traverse or lacerate tissue despite flowing blood. [12]

Because off-label occluders left residual fistulae, a dedicated device was developed. To test safety and exploratory effectiveness of a dedicated transcaval closure device, investigators noted that transcaval access enables delivery of large-caliber devices to the aorta in patients ineligible for transfemoral arterial access, but persistent aorto-caval fistulae at exit from the catheterization lab and bleeding complications were common in the prospective study. [13] Reassuringly, longer-term follow-up showed that there were no late vascular complications of transcaval access, and 93% of fistulas were proven occluded at last follow-up, with only one proven patent after 12 months. [14]

## Comparative Outcomes

Comparative data support transcaval access among nonfemoral options. In a propensity-weighted analysis, transcaval access had a lower rate of stroke/TIA than transaxillary access for TAVR, comparable bleeding and vascular complications, and a higher rate of discharge directly to home without stroke/TIA. [15] Importantly, as compared with transfemoral access, transcaval and transaxillary access were associated with worse outcomes, including worse bleeding, vascular complications, stroke or TIA, length of stay, and mortality. [15] The European registry confirmed feasibility: transcaval access was successful in 49 out of 50 patients and device success was obtained in 94% of cases, with closure of the caval-aortic puncture site successful in all cases without need for emergent surgery. [16] Single-center comparison against transapical and transaxillary approaches has also been reported. [17] A recent meta-analysis found that across 8 studies with 467 patients, transcaval TAVR achieved a success rate of 98.5% and a 30-day all-cause mortality rate of 6.1%. [18]

## Expanding Applications

Beyond TAVR, transcaval access has broadened. It has been used for thoracic endovascular aortic repair, where transcaval aortic access has been used for deployment of transcatheter aortic valves in patients in whom conventional arterial approaches are not feasible, and the report describes its use for TEVAR in a patient with a descending thoracic aneurysm. [19] It also supports mechanical circulatory support: transcaval access is feasible for emergency nonsurgical implantation of the Impella 5.0 device in cardiogenic shock with small or diseased iliofemoral arteries. [20] The technique now extends across the inferior vena cava–retroperitoneal–aortic route for multiple therapeutic procedures. [21] CT-based anatomic suitability assessment helps select candidates and avoid mesenteric or atheroembolic complications. [22] Foundational TAVR and access literature, electrosurgical principles, registry analyses, and procedural tutorials together frame the evidence base. [23–30]

## Conclusion

Transcaval access has matured from a counterintuitive bench concept into a validated, ergonomically familiar route for large-bore structural heart interventions when transfemoral access is unsuitable. Although outcomes remain inferior to transfemoral access, contemporary data—particularly lower stroke rates versus transaxillary access and reassuring tract healing—support its role in selected patients. Wider adoption awaits commercially available dedicated crossing and closure devices.
